name: Ozokerite mumioid

card.summary: Ozokerite, a natural mineral wax grouped with shilajit-like 'mumioids', used as a structuring wax in cosmetics such as lipsticks and in warm wax therapy for skin and joints.
card.note: Not the same material as shilajit despite a similar tarry appearance.

quick.overview:
Ozokerite, or earth wax, is a naturally occurring mixture of hydrocarbons that ranges from soft wax to a hard black mass. Wikipedia's shilajit article lists it among the mumioids, natural substances that resemble shilajit in appearance.

Its looks-related role is as a structuring wax in cosmetics: it is refined into ceresine, a wax used to give products such as lipsticks body and stability, and Russian-language medical literature has reviewed warm ozokerite applications as a therapy.
quick.how: In cosmetics it is blended with other waxes and oils as an ingredient, not applied raw. In therapy settings, melted ozokerite is applied warm to the body. Products sold as mumijo or shilajit are different substances.
quick.risks: Ozokerite as a cosmetic ingredient is a refined mineral wax. Products marketed as shilajit have been reported to contain heavy metals such as lead in some samples, so the name overlap is worth noting.

lead: Ozokerite, also called earth wax, is a naturally occurring odoriferous mineral wax; it is a mixture of hydrocarbons that melts at roughly 58 to 100 degrees Celsius and is classed as a mineraloid.[1] Commercial supply historically came largely from Galicia in the Carpathian region, with mining there beginning in the 1880s.[1]

It is refined into ceresine, long used in candles and electrical insulation and as an adulterant of beeswax.[1] In cosmetics, waxes serve as structuring agents in lipsticks, and studies of wax matrixes have examined ozokerite alongside beeswax and carnauba.[2][3] A 1988 Russian-language review covered ozokerite as a medical treatment.[4]

The term mumioid links it to shilajit: Wikipedia's shilajit article lists ozokerite among natural substances that resemble shilajit in appearance.[5] Shilajit itself is a different material, mostly humic substances formed in mountain rock crevices.[5]

chain: Refined wax is blended into cosmetics or applied warm
It gives structure to lip products and holds heat on skin

angle.text: Ozokerite appears as a wax in lipsticks and similar products, and is used warm in some therapy settings. The appearance benefit comes through the finished cosmetic or the skin comfort from heat.

paras: Ozokerite likely formed when petroleum evaporated and oxidised, leaving paraffin in fissures; its consistency ranges from soft wax to a very hard black mass.[1] Crude material is refined with sulfuric acid and charcoal into ceresine.[1]

Residues of ceresine have been found in Roman-era casting molds in the Moravian region, indicating earth wax was used for wax models in lost-wax casting.[6] Commercial mining in Galicia began in the 1880s and declined after 1940 as petroleum paraffins became more competitive.[1]

Lipsticks combine several waxes to provide stability, texture and pay-off, and researchers testing alternative waxes describe the need to replace petroleum-derived ones.[3] Laboratory work has compared ozokerite with beeswax and candelilla in wax matrixes, finding ozokerite and beeswax formed needle-like crystals that increased matrix strength.[2]
A 1988 review in a Russian medical journal discussed ozokerite treatment.[4]

Shilajit, also called mumijo, is a tar-like material of humic substances found in high mountain regions; some samples contain heavy metals including lead.[5] Ozokerite is listed among mumioids because of visual similarity, not shared composition.[5]
No studies found. A 1988 narrative review of ozokerite treatment exists in Russian-language literature.[4]

timeline.event: Commercial mining of ozokerite begins in Galicia.[1]
Mining declines as petroleum paraffins become competitive.[1]
